title: Teachable Machine
content_html:
What We're Doing

In this hands-on activity, students will build their very own image classifier using Google's Teachable Machine — a free browser-based tool that lets anyone train a real machine learning model without writing a single line of code. Students will use their device's webcam (or uploaded photos) to teach a model to recognise different categories of images, such as hand gestures, objects, or facial expressions.

By the end of the session, students will have a working AI model that can correctly identify what it "sees" in real time, and — more importantly — they will understand the core concepts behind how machine learning actually works: collecting data, training a model, testing its accuracy, and recognising bias when the model gets things wrong. This is a foundational lesson for understanding that AI systems are only as good as the data used to train them.

This is an intermediate-level session, so it assumes students already have basic familiarity with what AI is and have perhaps seen a demo of image recognition before. Here, they move from "watching AI work" to "building an AI model themselves."

Tools & Resources

  • Google Teachable Machine — https://teachablemachine.withgoogle.com/ (free, no login required, runs entirely in the browser; no data leaves the device unless exported)
  • A device with a webcam — laptop, tablet, or desktop with a working camera. If no webcam is available, students can upload image files instead.
  • Chrome or Edge browser (recommended for best camera permission handling; Teachable Machine may behave inconsistently on older browsers)
  • Optional: sample image folders pre-downloaded on a USB drive or shared folder, in case internet bandwidth is limited and students need to upload images instead of using live webcam capture
  • Free-tier limits to watch for: Teachable Machine is completely free with no account needed, but it runs entirely client-side, meaning large image classes or many samples can slow down or crash older/low-spec devices. Models are also not saved automatically to the cloud unless the student explicitly exports/downloads or uploads to Google Drive — remind students to save their work before closing the tab.

Step-by-Step Activity

  1. Open a browser and navigate to teachablemachine.withgoogle.com. Click "Get Started," then choose "Image Project," and select "Standard image model."
  2. Explain the interface: there are "Class" boxes on the left (where training images go), a "Training" panel in the middle, and a "Preview" panel on the right (where the live model will make predictions).
  3. Rename Class 1 and Class 2 to something meaningful — for example, "Thumbs Up" and "Thumbs Down," or "Book" and "Phone." Add a third class ("Nothing" or "Background") to help the model learn what "neither category" looks like.
  4. Click the webcam icon under each class box and grant camera permission when prompted by the browser.
  5. For each class, hold down the "Hold to Record" button to capture at least 50–100 images while varying angle, distance, lighting, and background. Repeat for every class.
  6. Click the "Train Model" button in the centre panel. Do not close the tab or switch away — training takes anywhere from 10 seconds to a few minutes depending on the number of images and device speed.
  7. Once training finishes, test the model live in the "Preview" panel by holding up the object/gesture in front of the webcam and watching the confidence percentages update in real time.
  8. Deliberately test with a "confusing" input — for example, an object that overlaps two classes or unusual lighting — and discuss why the model gets it wrong or right.
  9. Go back and add 20–30 more training images to the class that performed worst, focusing on varied conditions, then retrain and re-test to observe improvement.
  10. Export the model: click "Export Model," choose "Tensorflow.js," and either copy the shareable link or download the model files to keep a record of the finished project.
  11. Have each student (or pair) present their trained model to the class for 1 minute, showing what it classifies and one thing they discovered while training it.

Example Outputs

  • Gesture Classifier: A model trained on "Thumbs Up," "Thumbs Down," and "Open Palm" that correctly identifies each gesture with over 90% confidence, including when tested from different angles.
  • Object Sorter: A model that distinguishes between a "Water Bottle," "Notebook," and "Phone" placed on a desk, demonstrating that the model has learned shape and colour cues rather than just background context.
  • Expression Detector: A model trained on "Smiling Face," "Serious Face," and "Surprised Face" that reveals limitations — for instance, performing well on the student who trained it but poorly on a classmate with different facial features, sparking rich discussion on bias in training data.

Facilitation Tips

  • Do a live demo first before letting students loose — show one full cycle (collect → train → test) so they see the whole workflow before diving in themselves.
  • Encourage variety early: many students will collect all their training images sitting in the exact same position, which produces a model that fails the moment lighting or angle changes. Prompt them mid-activity to "move around, change the background, get closer and farther."
  • Watch device performance — if a laptop is old or many browser tabs are open, training can be slow. Suggest closing other tabs before starting.
  • Some students will get suspiciously perfect (100%) results initially — use this as a teaching moment: ask "would this still work if I stood by the window?" and test it live to reveal overfitting.
  • Camera permission pop-ups are a common stumbling block — walk the room early to make sure everyone has granted access before the training phase begins.
  • Keep training sample counts roughly balanced across classes; a common confusion is students recording 200 images for one class and 20 for another, which skews the model's predictions toward the larger class.
  • Plan for roughly: 10 min setup/demo, 15 min class naming and data collection, 10 min first training and testing, 15 min data improvement and retraining, 15 min export/sharing, remaining time for presentations and discussion.
  • If webcams are unavailable or unreliable, have a backup folder of pre-selected images ready so students can use the "upload" option instead of live capture.

Discussion Questions

  • What steps did the model go through between you showing it images and it being able to make predictions?
  • Why did the model perform differently when you changed the lighting, angle, or background — what does this tell you about how it "sees"?
  • If someone else used your trained model, do you think it would work as well for them as it did for you? Why or why not?
  • What is the difference between the model "memorising" your exact training images versus actually "learning" the category?
  • Where in daily life might a similar image classifier already be working behind the scenes — and what could go wrong if its training data was unfair or incomplete?

Extension Challenges

  • Easy: Add a fourth class to your existing model and retrain it — test whether adding more categories makes the model less accurate overall, and explain why.
  • Medium: Deliberately try to "break" your model by testing it with tricky inputs (poor lighting, partial objects, mixed backgrounds). Document at least three failure cases and propose a specific fix (e.g., more images, different angles) for each one.
  • Hard: Export your trained model's shareable link and swap with a partner. Test your partner's model using your own face/objects instead of theirs, record the accuracy drop, and write a short explanation of why the model behaves differently for a "new" user — connecting this to real-world concerns about AI systems trained on narrow or non-representative datasets.
